title: etbb-july-2024-may-2025-update.pdf — section 207
text:
35. These adjustments may help for many learning/developmental disabilities:
• Using short sentences and simple punctuation.
• Using uncomplicated language.
• Avoiding all jargon.
• Using “you” and “we” rather than third person.
• Using figures instead of spelling out numbers.
• Using bullet points for key points.
• Using sub-headings and allowing white space between sections.
• Using larger print, clear typeface, greater spacing, coloured paper.
• Using photos/drawings/concrete symbols to support text.
• Being careful about loss of formatting on emails.
• Using an easy language paragraph that summarises the decision. This is especially of
benefit to litigants with learning disorders or to children.154
• For written judgments, there are tools online to make language simpler and which will
assist judges to write for a person with poor literacy.155
• Where written or telephone communication is difficult, confusing or stressful, holding
additional case management preliminary hearings.
• Being more explicit with instructions, ie stating what appears to be obvious (eg precisely
to whom documents should be sent; explaining that “send to the respondent” means
“send to the respondent’s solicitor” if the respondent is represented).
• Avoiding making too many orders or giving too many instructions and tasks at once,
or which are to be completed at one time.
• Extending time limits for taking action.
• Allowing longer hearing times for case management/preliminary hearings.
